newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul financial reform plans stir union outcry.
newsitem.headline: Seoul financial reform plans stir union outcry.

text.p: Unionised workers at the central Bank of Korea on Monday demanded the bank's governor resign over his acceptance of a proposal to transfer bank supervisory authority to another branch of the government.
Workers said they suspected central bank governor Lee Kyung-shick of having been offered a government post or a ticket into politics in return for compromising on the issue.
"Governor Lee is suspected of having been offered a promise of help in his desire to enter politics," Park Chul-soo, spokesman for the bank's labour union, told Reuters.
"Otherwise, how could he dare to think of such a decision that runs counter to the very nature of the central bank?"

The controversy followed the announcement by Finance Minister Kang Kyong-shik that the existing banking, securities and insurance industry watchdog bodies would be integrated into a single organisation under the prime minister.
Lee told a news conference the final draft would not weaken the central bank's rights. He did not specifically comment on the union's demand to resign, and could not be reached later for comment.

Kang Kyong-shik told reporters there would be no job cuts "in the process of integrating the supervisory bodies", but did not elaborate how to absorb all the existing workforce into a single organisation.

Kang said the decision, which was part of the government's final draft for financial reforms, had been made after consulting governor Lee and the head of the Presidential Commission for Financial Reform, Park Seong-yawng.
In a rare public action, the bank's managerial staff members also issued a statement demanding the decision be scrapped.

"(The decision) makes it impossible for the central bank to implement its intrinsic function and runs counter to a global trend of strengthening the central bank's supervisory authority over banks," the statement said.

Labour unions at the Securities Supervisory Board and the Insurance Supervisory Board said they supported the Bank of Korea's union, arguing the government was trying to gain control over the whole financial industry in an election year.
President Kim Young-sam's single term expires next February, and presidential elections are scheduled for December.
Analysts played down the union's accusations and said workers were really worried about losing their jobs as a result of integration of the watchdog bodies.

"It's a global trend that barriers between financial sectors are falling," said Kim Min-tae, an analyst at LG Economic Research Institute. "I think the basic idea of integrating the supervisory functions is well in line with this trend." The draft also stipulated that the Bank of Korea's
governor would replace the finance minister as the head of the Monetary Board, the top monetary policy-making body, and that government officials would be banned from sitting on the board.

In return for increased autonomy, the central bank governor would be asked to set annual targets for inflation and other macroeconomic indicators and would be held responsible for meeting those targets, Kang said.
President Kim on Saturday approved the draft, prepared on the basis of discussions by the presidential commission which was formed in January to review the financial industry reform.

However, Kang did not mention raising the ceiling of individual ownership in banks from the current four percent, another key issue. The commission earlier said the limit could be increased to 10 percent under certain conditions.

Share prices of major banks fell on Monday as investors were disappointed at the lack of dicussion on the ownership issue. The banking sub-index fell 2.34 percent, or 10.18 points, to close Monday's trading at 424.84 points.
The composite stock index closed down 2.92 points to 789.05.
